stories.title: The kitchen on Rue d'Arzew
stories.prompt: Describe the kitchen of the house where you grew up.

segments.text: Oh, the kitchen. It was tiny, and it was always too hot.
There was a blue tiled wall behind the stove, and my mother had hung a calendar from the bakery, always on the wrong month.
At Easter she made the mouna, a big round brioche with orange blossom water.
The whole street could smell it. Simone, my best friend, used to come and sit on the step just to wait for the first slice.
I was not allowed to touch the dough. So of course I touched the dough.
My mother pretended not to see. She always pretended not to see.
Even now, when I smell orange blossom, I am seven years old again, on that little stool by the window.

stories.title: The dance where I met Henri
stories.prompt: Who played the music at the Saturday dance, and who did you go with?

segments.text: It was a Saturday in June, at the dance hall in Saint-Cyprien. Simone dragged me there, I did not want to go.
Marcel played the accordion. He was terrible, but nobody cared, everybody danced anyway.
And there was this tall boy by the door who did not dance at all. He just watched.
After an hour he finally came to me and asked, very seriously, if I could teach him the waltz.
He stepped on my feet maybe twenty times. I counted.
At the end of the night he said, next Saturday I will be better. And he was not better. But he came back every Saturday.
That was Henri. We were married three years later, and he never learned to waltz.

stories.title: My first classroom
stories.prompt: Tell me about your very first day as a teacher.

segments.text: My first school was in a village in the Ariège mountains. One room, thirty-one children, from six years old to fourteen.
In winter I had to light the stove myself at seven in the morning, otherwise the ink froze in the inkwells.
On the first day, a little boy called Pierrot came in with a hedgehog in his coat pocket.
He said it was his cousin. The whole class laughed, and I laughed too, and that was the end of being a strict teacher.
I stayed in that village four years. I still receive a postcard from Pierrot every Christmas. He is a grandfather now.

stories.title: The blue 2CV and the tractor
stories.prompt: Claire added a photo of you in front of a blue 2CV. Tell me about that day.

segments.text: Ah, Claire found that photo! That was the summer of seventy-six, the year it was so hot.
Henri decided we would drive to the sea at Collioure, with Claire who was two years old, in our little blue 2CV.
The car broke down in the middle of the vineyards. Nothing, nobody, just the cicadas.
And then a farmer arrived on his tractor, as if it was the most normal thing in the world, and he pulled us all the way to the village.
Claire sat on Henri's knees and she shouted at every car that passed. She thought it was the best day of her life.
We never saw the sea that day. But we ate peaches with the farmer's family, and honestly, it was better than the sea.

stories.title: Henri's bicycle to Barcelona
stories.prompt: Lucas wants to know: did Grandpa ever do something crazy when he was young?

segments.text: Lucas asked that? Oh, he will like this one.
The summer after we met, I went to Barcelona for a month, to help my aunt in her shop.
Henri had no money for the train. So he took his bicycle. Toulouse to Barcelona, over the Pyrenees, on a bicycle with three gears.
It took him five days. He arrived at my aunt's shop completely burnt by the sun, with one shoe.
My aunt looked at him and said to me, in Spanish, this one, you keep him.
So tell Lucas: his grandfather was not crazy. He was in love. It is almost the same thing.

stories.title: The night Claire was born
stories.prompt: What do you remember about the day your first child was born?

segments.text: Claire was born in March, during the biggest storm of the year. All the lights in the street went out.
Henri drove me to the hospital with one hand on the wheel and the other holding an umbrella out of the window, I still do not know why.
She arrived at four in the morning, very small and very angry.
The nurse said, this one will have opinions. And she was right, Claire has had opinions ever since.
When they put her in my arms, the electricity came back, all at once. Henri said it was a sign. He said that about everything.
